index.title: Reverse-Mode Autodiff by Hand
index.prompt: Autograd is bookkeeping. Keep the books yourself, in NumPy, for f(x, y) = (xy + x) sigmoid(y). First derive each partial derivative in closed form from a backward walk on paper, then run the same walk as a tape: store every intermediate of the forward pass, visit the steps in reverse, give each step's inputs their share of the adjoint, and add rather than overwrite when a variable is used twice.
index.answer: Auto-graded inside the notebook. The closed forms must match a central difference to 1e-5 without collapsing either of the two routes that x and y take through the graph, and the tape must reproduce f, give df/dx = 0.933689 and df/dy = 1.462447 at (1.5, 0.5), and agree with the closed forms to 1e-9 at five random points.

index.title: Define-by-Run, Defined
index.prompt: PyTorch is called a define-by-run framework. Which description fits?
index.answer: Each operation runs at once on real values and is recorded as it goes, so the graph is whatever the Python code executed, branches and loops included. The graph exists only for the pass that built it. backward() uses it once, and the next forward pass records a fresh one from whatever code runs that time.

index.title: The Job of a Central Difference
index.prompt: The central difference (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / 2h estimates a derivative from two values of f near x. What is it for?
index.answer: Checking a gradient, whether from a derivation or from autograd, to five or six digits. This is the standard gradient check. With h near 10 to the minus 6 in float64 the estimate matches a correct gradient to five or six digits, and a disagreement points at a mistake in the derivation or the code.

index.title: What requires_grad Switches On
index.prompt: You create a tensor with requires_grad=True. What does that setting change?
index.answer: PyTorch starts recording the operations applied to the tensor, so a later backward() can work out a gradient for it. The recorded operations form the computation graph. backward() walks that graph from the result back to the tensor and leaves the gradient in its grad field.

index.title: Why the Sweep Runs Backward
index.prompt: Training needs the gradient of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters, and autograd computes it in reverse mode. Why not forward mode?
index.answer: The loss is a single number, so one backward sweep delivers the gradient for every parameter at once. Forward mode pushes a derivative through from one input at a time, so it would take one sweep per parameter, millions of them. Reverse mode starts at the single output and reaches every input in one pass that costs a small multiple of the forward pass.
